body_md:
Amanda Seyfried has revealed the unusual secrecy surrounding her participation in You Can See Everything, the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Appearing on Jimmy Fallon's Tonight Show, the actress described joining the production late and having remarkably limited access to its materials before filming.

According to Seyfried, the documentary had largely taken shape before she became involved, and her participation transformed aspects of the project. She recalled that she might only be able to read the script the night before filming through an application she described as requiring five-factor authentication. Her description conveys the extent of the secrecy, although the precise technical security measures have not been independently established.

Seyfried previously portrayed Holmes in Hulu's The Dropout, winning an Emmy for that performance. Her involvement in the documentary presented a different creative challenge. After Holmes was incarcerated, Fielder recruited Seyfried to reenact parts of the narrative. The actress appears both as Holmes and as herself, contributing to a production that combines documentary material with performed reconstruction.

The actress explained that Holmes's highly public profile provided abundant research material. However, the documentary's own footage of Holmes during the period covered by the filmmakers was not available to Seyfried until she arrived on set. That distinction meant she could prepare using familiar public material but could not fully anticipate how the documentary would present its subject or incorporate her performance.

Distributor A24 initially kept Seyfried's involvement under wraps and asked reviewers not to reveal the surprise. The report also states that the documentary has surpassed $100 million at the worldwide box office, an unusual commercial milestone for a production in this format. Its unconventional structure has generated considerable discussion about the boundaries of documentary filmmaking.

Seyfried's participation has also prompted speculation about whether a performance within a documentary might receive recognition in acting awards categories. Such discussion should not be confused with confirmation of eligibility, a nomination or an eventual Oscar victory. Her previous Emmy-winning portrayal makes the possibility particularly interesting, but any awards outcome remains uncertain.

Beyond the secrecy surrounding the screenplay, the project raises broader questions about the relationship between recorded reality and dramatic interpretation. By incorporating an actress who has already portrayed its central real-life figure, the film offers an unusual example of how nonfiction storytelling can interact with an existing screen performance.
